title: JavaScript Promises versus Task
hook: Both models let you write linear async code. The scheduling underneath is not the same: Promises settle into the microtask queue on one JS thread; Tasks resume on a .NET thread-pool thread unless a SynchronizationContext says otherwise.

sections.heading: What maps, and what does not
sections.prose: A JS Promise is a thenable object that is pending, fulfilled, or rejected. A .NET Task is a thenable in spirit: incomplete, ran-to-completion, faulted, or canceled. await promise in JS schedules a microtask; those microtasks drain before the next macrotask (timers, I/O callbacks). await task in C# schedules a continuation that may run on another thread. There is no microtask queue in the CLR. That is why a long CPU loop in a JS async function freezes the UI or the Node event loop, while a long CPU loop inside a C# async method after an await still freezes that thread but other pool threads can proceed. JS has no ValueTask; every async function allocates a Promise. JS has no CancellationToken on the language Promise; AbortSignal is bolted onto fetch and friends.

snippets.label: Same composition, different scheduler
snippets.explanation: WhenAll is Promise.all. Continuations may hop threads. In JS, the then callbacks still run on the single JS thread via microtasks.

sections.heading: Interview trap: ‘async means parallel’
sections.prose: In both languages, awaiting A then B is sequential. Starting both then combining is concurrent wait. Parallel CPU in JS requires Worker threads or a native addon; in C# it requires extra threads (Task.Run, Parallel, PLINQ) which is module 15, not this language TAP module. TypeScript’s Promise types erase; Task<T> remains in IL and is awaited by the state machine. Do not say ‘Task is just a Promise.’ Say ‘same programmer model, different execution engine.’

interviewTakeaways: Promise continuations are microtasks on one thread; Task continuations are pool threads unless marshaled.
Promise.all ≈ Task.WhenAll; neither is data parallelism.
AbortController is the practical JS analog of CancellationToken, not a hidden field on Promise.
commonPitfalls: Claiming C# await uses a microtask queue.
Using Task.Result in a WhenAll continuation and thinking it is as safe as awaiting (it is OK after WhenAll completes, but the style hides faults if WhenAll is skipped).
Equating Node worker_threads with C# async/await.

jsTsCorrelations.note: queueMicrotask and Promise.then always run on the JS thread before rendering or I/O macrotasks. Map this against Task continuations that can run on any pool thread.
TypeScript’s Promise<T> is a compile-time annotation around a JS Promise. Task<T> is a real CLR type with status, cancellation, and exception storage.
